processing: A pan-fired green tea that puts great weight on firing: long frying at low temperature builds the chestnut aroma and a leaf that holds up to repeated steeps.
harvest_season: Spring is usual for pan-fired greens of the class; no exact picking calendar is documented for this tea.
appearance_dry: Tight, glossy strips in a greyish green.
taste_profile: A high, lasting chestnut aroma with a fresh, mellow taste and a sweet return, sturdier than most tender greens.

brewing.notes: It takes hotter water and more steeps than a delicate bud tea, since it is known for lasting well in the pot.

vintage_note: As is usual for Chinese green teas it is sold by the current year's harvest and best drunk within the year. Its firing makes it a little more forgiving than bud teas, but it is not a tea to age.
description:
Pingshan Chaoqing is a pan-fired green tea from Pingshan county in Yibin, on the north bank of the lower Jinsha River. 'Chaoqing' just means wok-fired green, a plain working style, and Pingshan's version is known for being sturdier and more aromatic than the word suggests.

The key is the firing. Makers keep the heat low and the frying long, which gives strong chestnut notes and a tea that stands up to several steeps. The registered area spans 16 townships at roughly 600 to 1,000 metres, on mountain yellow soils.

Expect tight grey-green strips, a bright yellow-green liquor, and a fresh, mellow taste with a sweet finish. Use slightly hotter water than for a bud tea, and do not be afraid of a fourth steep.

It is a protected geographical indication, and the same local producers also sell a finer tea called Longhu Cui, so do not confuse the two. Look for tight, unbroken strips and a clean chestnut smell without scorch.
history:
Pingshan was formerly known as Pingyi county and Mahu prefecture, and the Jiajing-era Mahu gazetteer of the Ming dynasty records that Pingyi produced tea. Local writers trace use of wild tea here back to the Eastern Han, but that claim is hard to pin down.

The tea's documented modern record starts in 1984, when it began twelve consecutive listings as a quality green tea of Sichuan province. It also served as Sichuan's sample tea for the pan-fired class, and work on standardising its making won a Yibin city science award in 2007.
